title: Letter and Verdict
premise: Ines Thackeray built her true-crime podcast on the 1998 disappearance of schoolteacher Mara Voss, a case the coastal town of Greywater sealed shut with a verdict of accidental drowning. When a corpse surfaces in the tidal marsh wearing clothes taken from Ines's own closet—clothes only someone who had been inside her house could have stolen—the town's old guard closes ranks, and Ines realizes her fifteen years of quiet archiving made her both witness and suspect. Following a hidden letter from the original coroner, she uncovers that Mara's death was staged by three men who now run the town, and that the body in her clothes is the last person who tried to expose them. In the climax, Ines lures the killers into confessing on a live broadcast from the marsh at low tide; justice arrives not through the compromised courts but through the town itself finally listening, and the tide gives up what it took.
about_author: Orsen Okafor is a former court reporter who spent a decade transcribing small-town trials before turning to fiction. He writes mysteries about records, silence, and the people who keep both.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of the Dead
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. She introduces her podcast and her meticulous archive of Greywater's secrets, then gets the call: a body in the marsh wearing her own missing cardigan. The emotional beat is the shattering of her carefully ordered invisibility—the archivist becomes an exhibit.

chapters.title: Closed for Good
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. At the police station, Detective Rennick—a man whose career was built on the Voss verdict—treats her as a suspect rather than a victim. Flashbacks to 1998 reveal how quickly the case was closed. Beat: dread as she realizes the machinery of the town is turning against her.

chapters.title: What the Closet Kept
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Searching her home, she finds signs of a careful intruder and discovers the dead man is Daniel Pryce, a retired clerk who once mailed her anonymous research tips. Beat: guilt and vertigo—her sources are dying, and her archive may have marked them.

chapters.title: The Coroner's Letter
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Ines and letters written by coroner Elias Brandt before his own 'accidental' death in 2001. His letter names discrepancies in Mara Voss's autopsy. Beat: hope igniting into obsession as the cold case cracks open.

chapters.title: Three Pillars
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. She maps the letter's clues onto Greywater's founding families: Judge Aldous Crane, developer Silas Marsh, and Sheriff-turned-councilman Tom Beake. Each is charming, powerful, untouchable. Beat: cold clarity about power's architecture—and her own powerlessness inside it.

chapters.title: Low Water
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, with interludes from Mara's sister Ruth, who never believed the verdict. A midnight search of the marsh uncovers Mara's satchel, preserved in the mud, containing evidence Brandt hid. Beat: grief and resolve fused; the past physically surfacing.

chapters.title: A Visit from the Judge
chapters.summary: Crane's POV for the first time. He offers Ines money, legacy, a seat at the table—then threatens her archive, her listeners, her life. Beat: seduction curdling into menace; the reader sees corruption wearing a civilized face.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Her studio burns; her backup drives vanish; Rennick warns her to leave town or join Pryce. But Ruth reveals Mara was pregnant, and the father's name appears in Brandt's letter—one of the three. Beat: betrayal sharpened into purpose.

chapters.title: The Tide Table
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. She plans the trap: a live broadcast from the marsh at spring low tide, timed when the pillars must retrieve the satchel themselves. She wires herself, alerts every listener, and accepts she may not walk out. Beat: terrified calm before the storm.

chapters.title: Verdict
chapters.summary: Climax and resolution, Ines's POV. On air, the men come for the satchel and confess within earshot of thousands; Rennick, finally choosing conscience, arrests them as the crowd arrives. Weeks later, the case is reopened, Mara buried properly, and Ines files her archive under a new heading: truth. Beat: justice outside the law, then within it—grief answered, silence broken.
